title: Völuspá
source: Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to) page images via handrit.is + Guðni Jónsson's Old Norse via heimskringla.no + Thorpe (1866) English
description: Völuspá, from the Poetic Edda in Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), fol. 1r-3r. Each section links the manuscript page that carries its stanzas. Old Norse from Guðni Jónsson's edition (heimskringla.no); English by Benjamin Thorpe (1866, public domain).
introduction:
Völuspá is preserved in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, Árni Magnússon Institute, Reykjavík), an Icelandic parchment book written about 1270. The poem fills fol. 1r-3r (manuscript pages 1-5).

Pages: each section holds the stanzas that begin on one manuscript page and links that page's photograph (handrit.is); a stanza that runs onto the next page links both pages. The page of every stanza comes from Wimmer and Finnur Jónsson's 1891 diplomatic edition, which prints the text of each manuscript page, and the first line of every page was checked on the photograph. 'Where on the image' under each section gives the details.

Texts: the Old Norse is Guðni Jónsson's normalized edition (via heimskringla.no), a reading text in modern spelling, not a letter-by-letter transcription of the manuscript; in places it adds words or lines from other manuscripts and follows modern editions where they rearrange stanzas. The English is Benjamin Thorpe's 1866 translation (public domain). The prose passages of the manuscript are not included.

Not in the manuscript: Stanza 54 (the Garmr refrain) is not written at this point in Codex Regius: on fol. 2v stanza 53 is followed directly by stanza 55. Guðni Jónsson repeats the refrain here after Hauksbók. Stanza 65 (Þá kemr inn ríki) is not in Codex Regius: on fol. 3r stanza 64 is followed directly by stanza 66. Guðni Jónsson's text takes it from Hauksbók (AM 544 4to); fol. 3r is linked because that is where the stanza would stand.

Stanza order: On fol. 2v the manuscript order is 47, refrain (abbreviated 'Geyr nú g.'), 50, 51, 48, 52, 53, 55, 56, 57, refrain ('Geyr n.'), 59-64; the edition moves stanza 48 and writes the refrain out in full as stanzas 49 and 58.

English alignment: Thorpe printed the middle of the poem in a different order from the manuscript, and the old version of this entry set his stanzas beside the wrong Old Norse stanzas from stanza 21 on. Each Thorpe stanza now stands beside the Old Norse stanza it translates. His numbers differ as follows (Old Norse = Thorpe): 21=25, 22=26, 23=27, 24=28, 25=29, 26=30, 27=31, 28=21+22, 29=23, 30=24, 31=36, 32-33=37, 34=39, 35=38, 36=40, 37=41, 38=42, 39=43, 40=32, 41=33, 42=34, 43=35, 45=45+46, 46=47, 47=48 (which also renders the Garmr refrain), 48=52, 50=49, 51=50, 52=51, 55=54, 56=55, 57=56, 59=57, 60=58, 61=59, 62=60, 63=61, 64=62, 65=64, 66=65. Thorpe has no separate English for the repeated refrain (49, 54, 58), and his translation lacks parts of stanzas 32-33 (Baldrs bróðir ... Baldrs andskota).

translation.original_text: <sup>1</sup>Hljóðs bið ek allar / helgar kindir, / meiri ok minni / mögu Heimdallar; / viltu at ek, Valföðr, / vel fyr telja / forn spjöll fira, / þau er fremst of man. <sup>2</sup>Ek man jötna / ár of borna, / þá er forðum mik / fædda höfðu; / níu man ek heima, / níu íviðjur, / mjötvið mæran / fyr mold neðan. <sup>3</sup>Ár var alda, / þat er ekki var, / var-a sandr né sær / né svalar unnir; / jörð fannsk æva / né upphiminn, / gap var ginnunga / en gras hvergi. <sup>4</sup>Áðr Burs synir / bjöðum of yppðu, / þeir er Miðgarð / mæran skópu; / sól skein sunnan / á salar steina, / þá var grund gróin / grænum lauki. <sup>5</sup>Sól varp sunnan, / sinni mána, / hendi inni hægri / um himinjöður; / sól þat né vissi, / hvar hon sali átti, / máni þat né vissi, / hvat hann megins átti, / stjörnur þat né vissu / hvar þær staði áttu. <sup>6</sup>Þá gengu regin öll / á rökstóla, / ginnheilög goð, / ok um þat gættusk; / nótt ok niðjum / nöfn of gáfu, / morgin hétu / ok miðjan dag, / undorn ok aftan, / árum at telja. <sup>7</sup>Hittusk æsir / á Iðavelli, / þeir er hörg ok hof / hátimbruðu; / afla lögðu, / auð smíðuðu, / tangir skópu / ok tól gerðu. <sup>8</sup>Tefldu í túni, / teitir váru, / var þeim vettergis / vant ór gulli, / uns þrjár kvámu / þursa meyjar / ámáttkar mjök / ór Jötunheimum. <sup>9</sup>Þá gengu regin öll / á rökstóla, / ginnheilög goð, / ok um þat gættusk, / hverir skyldi dverga / dróttir skepja / ór Brimis blóði / ok ór Bláins leggjum. <sup>10</sup>Þar var Móðsognir / mæztr of orðinn / dverga allra, / en Durinn annarr; / þeir mannlíkun / mörg of gerðu / dvergar í jörðu, / sem Durinn sagði. <sup>11</sup>Nýi, Niði, / Norðri, Suðri, / Austri, Vestri, / Alþjófr, Dvalinn, / Nár ok Náinn / Nípingr, Dáinn / Bívurr, Bávurr, / Bömburr, Nóri, / Ánn ok Ánarr, / Óinn, Mjöðvitnir. <sup>12</sup>Veggr ok Gandalfr, / Vindalfr, Þorinn, / Þrár ok Þráinn, / Þekkr, Litr ok Vitr, / Nýr ok Nýráðr, / nú hefi ek dverga, / Reginn ok Ráðsviðr, / rétt of talða. <sup>13</sup>Fíli, Kíli, / Fundinn, Náli, / Hefti, Víli, / Hannar, Svíurr, / Billingr, Brúni, / Bíldr ok Buri, / Frár, Hornbori, / Frægr ok Lóni, / Aurvangr, Jari, / Eikinskjaldi. <sup>14</sup>Mál er dverga / í Dvalins liði / ljóna kindum / til Lofars telja, / þeir er sóttu / frá salar steini / Aurvanga sjöt / til Jöruvalla. <sup>15</sup>Þar var Draupnir / ok Dolgþrasir, / Hár, Haugspori, / Hlévangr, Glóinn, / Dóri, Óri / Dúfr, Andvari / Skirfir, Virfir, / Skáfiðr, Ái. <sup>16</sup>Alfr ok Yngvi, / Eikinskjaldi, / Fjalarr ok Frosti, / Finnr ok Ginnarr; / þat mun æ uppi / meðan öld lifir, / langniðja tal / Lofars hafat.
translation.text: <sup>1</sup>For silence I pray all sacred children, great and small, sons of Heimdall, they will that I Valfather's deeds recount, men's ancient saws, those that I best remember. <sup>2</sup>The Jötuns I remember early born, those who me of old have reared. I nine worlds remember, nine trees, the great central tree, beneath the earth. <sup>3</sup>There was in times of old, where Ymir dwelt, nor sand nor sea, nor gelid waves; earth existed not, nor heaven above, 'twas a chaotic chasm, and grass nowhere. <sup>4</sup>Before Bur's sons raised up heaven's vault, they who the noble mid-earth shaped. The sun shone from the south over the structure's rocks: then was the earth begrown with herbage green. <sup>5</sup>The sun from the south, the moon's companion, her right hand cast about the heavenly horses. The sun knew not where she a dwelling had, the moon knew not what power he possessed, the stars knew not where they had a station. <sup>6</sup>Then went the powers all to their judgment-seats, the all-holy gods, and thereon held council: to night and to the waning moon gave names; morn they named, and mid-day, afternoon and eve, whereby to reckon years. <sup>7</sup>The Æsir met on Ida's plain; they altar-steads and temples high constructed; their strength they proved, all things tried, furnaces established, precious things forged, formed tongs, and fabricated tools; <sup>8</sup>At tables played at home; joyous they were; to them was naught the want of gold, until there came Thurs-maidens three, all powerful, from Jötunheim. <sup>9</sup>Then went all the powers to their judgment-seats, the all-holy gods, and thereon held council, who should of the dwarfs the race create, from the sea-giant's blood and livid bones. <sup>10</sup>Then was Môtsognir created greatest of all the dwarfs, and Durin second; there in man's likeness they created many dwarfs from earth, as Durin said. <sup>11</sup>Nýi and Nidi, Nordri and Sudri, Austri and Vestri, Althiôf, Dvalin Nâr and Nâin, Niping, Dain, Bivör, Bavör, Bömbur, Nori, An and Anar, Ai, Miodvitnir, <sup>12</sup>Veig and Gandâlf, Vindâlf, Thrain, Thekk and Thorin, Thrôr, Vitr, and Litr, Nûr and Nýrâd, Regin and Râdsvid. Now of the dwarfs I have rightly told. <sup>13</sup>Fili, Kili, Fundin, Nali, Hepti, Vili, Hanar, Svior, Billing, Bruni, Bild, Bûri, Frâr, Hornbori, Fræg and Lôni, Aurvang, Iari, Eikinskialdi. <sup>14</sup>Time 'tis of the dwarfs in Dvalin's band, to the sons of men, to Lofar up to reckon, those who came forth from the world's rock, earth's foundation, to Iora's plains. <sup>15</sup>There were Draupnir, and Dôlgthrasir, Hâr, Haugspori, Hlævang, Glôi, Skirvir, Virvir, Skafid, Ai, Alf and Yngvi, Eikinskialdi, <sup>16</sup>Fialar and Frosti, Finn and Ginnar, Heri, Höggstari, Hliôdôlf, Moin: that above shall, while mortals live, the progeny of Lofar, accounted be.
translation.scan_note: Fol. 1r (manuscript page 1; handrit.is image 10; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 1, caption 'Vǫluspá v. 1-15'): stanzas 1-16 begin here; stanza 16 runs on to fol. 1v. Fol. 1v (manuscript page 2; handrit.is image 11; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 2, caption 'Vǫluspá v. 15-31'): the top of the page finishes stanza 16 ('meðan öld lifir ...'). Checked on the image: the first line of fol. 1r has 'Hljóðs bið ek allar' (Völuspá 1); the first line of fol. 1v has 'meðan öld lifir' (end of Völuspá 16). In stanza 15 the edition's names Dóri, Óri, Dúfr, Andvari are not in Codex Regius; on fol. 1r the list runs Draupnir, Dolgþrasir, Hár, Haugspori, Hlévangr, Glói, Skirvir, Virvir, Skafiðr, Ái (Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 1).

translation.original_text: <sup>17</sup>Unz þrír kvámu / ór því liði / öflgir ok ástkir / æsir at húsi, / fundu á landi / lítt megandi / Ask ok Emblu / örlöglausa. <sup>18</sup>Önd þau né áttu, / óð þau né höfðu, / lá né læti / né litu góða; / önd gaf Óðinn, / óð gaf Hænir, / lá gaf Lóðurr / ok litu góða. <sup>19</sup>Ask veit ek standa, / heitir Yggdrasill, / hár baðmr, ausinn / hvíta auri; / þaðan koma döggvar, / þærs í dala falla, / stendr æ yfir grænn / Urðarbrunni. <sup>20</sup>Þaðan koma meyjar / margs vitandi / þrjár ór þeim sæ, / er und þolli stendr; / Urð hétu eina, / aðra Verðandi, / - skáru á skíði, - / Skuld ina þriðju; / þær lög lögðu, / þær líf kuru / alda börnum, / örlög seggja. <sup>21</sup>Þat man hon folkvíg / fyrst í heimi, / er Gullveigu / geirum studdu / ok í höll Hárs / hana brenndu, / þrisvar brenndu, / þrisvar borna, / oft, ósjaldan, / þó hon enn lifir. <sup>22</sup>Heiði hana hétu / hvars til húsa kom, / völu velspáa, / vitti hon ganda; / seið hon, hvars hon kunni, / seið hon hug leikinn, / æ var hon angan / illrar brúðar. <sup>23</sup>Þá gengu regin öll / á rökstóla, / ginnheilög goð, / ok um þat gættusk, / hvárt skyldu æsir / afráð gjalda / eða skyldu goðin öll / gildi eiga. <sup>24</sup>Fleygði Óðinn / ok í folk of skaut, / þat var enn folkvíg / fyrst í heimi; / brotinn var borðveggr / borgar ása, / knáttu vanir vígspá / völlu sporna. <sup>25</sup>Þá gengu regin öll / á rökstóla, / ginnheilög goð, / ok um þat gættusk, / hverjir hefði loft allt / lævi blandit / eða ætt jötuns / Óðs mey gefna. <sup>26</sup>Þórr einn þar vá / þrunginn móði, / - hann sjaldan sitr - / er hann slíkt of fregn -: / á gengusk eiðar, / orð ok særi, / mál öll meginlig, / er á meðal fóru. <sup>27</sup>Veit hon Heimdallar / hljóð of folgit / und heiðvönum / helgum baðmi, / á sér hon ausask / aurgum forsi / af veði Valföðrs. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>28</sup>Ein sat hon úti, / þá er inn aldni kom / yggjungr ása / ok í augu leit. / Hvers fregnið mik? / Hví freistið mín? / Allt veit ek, Óðinn, / hvar þú auga falt, / í inum mæra / Mímisbrunni. / Drekkr mjöð Mímir / morgun hverjan / af veði Valföðrs. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>29</sup>Valði henni Herföðr / hringa ok men, / fekk spjöll spaklig / ok spá ganda, / sá hon vítt ok of vítt / of veröld hverja. <sup>30</sup>Sá hon valkyrjur / vítt of komnar, / görvar at ríða / til Goðþjóðar; / Skuld helt skildi, / en Skögul önnur, / Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul / ok Geirskögul. / Nú eru talðar / nönnur Herjans, / görvar at ríða / grund valkyrjur.
translation.text: <sup>17</sup>Until there came three mighty and benevolent Æsir to the world from their assembly. They found on earth, nearly powerless, Ask and Embla, void of destiny. <sup>18</sup>Spirit they possessed not, sense they had not, blood nor motive powers, nor goodly colour. Spirit gave Odin, sense gave Hoenir, blood gave Lodur, and goodly colour. <sup>19</sup>I know an ash standing Yggdrasil hight, a lofty tree, laved with limpid water: thence come the dews into the dales that fall; ever stands it green over Urd's fountain. <sup>20</sup>Thence come maidens, much knowing, three from the hall, which under that tree stands; Urd hight the one, the second Verdandi,--on a tablet they graved--Skuld the third. Laws they established, life allotted to the sons of men; destinies pronounced. <sup>21</sup>She that war remembers, the first on earth, when Gullveig they with lances pierced, and in the high one's hall her burnt, thrice burnt, thrice brought her forth, oft not seldom; yet she still lives. <sup>22</sup>Heidi they called her, whithersoe'r she came, the well-foreseeing Vala: wolves she tamed, magic arts she knew, magic arts practised; ever was she the joy of evil people. <sup>23</sup>Then went the powers all to their judgment-seats, the all-holy gods, and thereon held council, whether the Æsir should avenge the crime, or all the gods receive atonement. <sup>24</sup>Broken was the outer wall of the Æsir's burgh. The Vanir, foreseeing conflict, tramp o'er the plains. Odin cast [his spear], and mid the people hurled it: that was the first warfare in the world. <sup>25</sup>Then went the powers all to their judgment-seats, the all-holy gods, and thereon held council: who had all the air with evil mingled? or to the Jötun race Od's maid had given? <sup>26</sup>There alone was Thor with anger swollen. He seldom sits, when of the like he hears. Oaths are not held sacred; nor words, nor swearing, nor binding compacts reciprocally made. <sup>27</sup>She knows that Heimdall's horn is hidden under the heaven-bright holy tree. A river she sees flow, with foamy fall, from Valfather's pledge. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>28</sup>Alone she sat without, when came that ancient dread Æsir's prince; and in his eye she gazed. "Of what wouldst thou ask me? Why temptest thou me? Odin! I know all, where thou thine eye didst sink in the pure well of Mim." Mim drinks mead each morn from Valfather's pledge. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>29</sup>The chief of hosts gave her rings and necklace, useful discourse, and a divining spirit: wide and far she saw o'er every world. <sup>30</sup>She the Valkyriur saw from afar coming, ready to ride to the god's people: Skuld held a shield, Skögul was second, then Gunn, Hild Göndul, and Geirskögul. Now are enumerated Herian's maidens, the Valkyriur, ready over the earth to ride.

translation.original_text: <sup>31</sup>Ek sá Baldri, / blóðgum tívur, / Óðins barni, / örlög folgin; / stóð of vaxinn / völlum hæri / mjór ok mjök fagr / mistilteinn. <sup>32</sup>Varð af þeim meiði, / er mær sýndisk, / harmflaug hættlig, / Höðr nam skjóta; / Baldrs bróðir var / of borinn snemma, / sá nam Óðins sonr / einnættr vega. <sup>33</sup>Þó hann æva hendr / né höfuð kembði, / áðr á bál of bar / Baldrs andskota; / en Frigg of grét / í Fensölum / vá Valhallar. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>34</sup>Þá kná Váli / vígbönd snúa, / heldr váru harðgör / höft ór þörmum. <sup>35</sup>Haft sá hon liggja / und Hveralundi, / lægjarns líki / Loka áþekkjan; / þar sitr Sigyn / þeygi of sínum / ver vel glýjuð. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>36</sup>Á fellur austan / um eitrdala / söxum ok sverðum, / Slíðr heitir sú. <sup>37</sup>Stóð fyr norðan / á Niðavöllum / salr ór gulli / Sindra ættar; / en annarr stóð / á Ókólni / bjórsalr jötuns, / en sá Brimir heitir. <sup>38</sup>Sal sá hon standa / sólu fjarri / Náströndu á, / norðr horfa dyrr; / falla eitrdropar / inn um ljóra, / sá er undinn salr / orma hryggjum. <sup>39</sup>Sá hon þar vaða / þunga strauma / menn meinsvara / ok morðvarga / ok þann er annars glepr / eyrarúnu; / þar saug Niðhöggr / nái framgengna, / sleit vargr vera. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>40</sup>Austr sat in aldna / í Járnviði / ok fæddi þar / Fenris kindir; / verðr af þeim öllum / einna nokkurr / tungls tjúgari / í trölls hami. <sup>41</sup>Fyllisk fjörvi / feigra manna, / rýðr ragna sjöt / rauðum dreyra; / svört verða sólskin / um sumur eftir, / veðr öll válynd. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>42</sup>Sat þar á haugi / ok sló hörpu / gýgjar hirðir, / glaðr Eggþér; / gól of hánum / í galgviði / fagrrauðr hani, / sá er Fjalarr heitir. <sup>43</sup>Gól of ásum / Gullinkambi, / sá vekr hölða / at Herjaföðrs; / en annarr gelr / fyr jörð neðan / sótrauðr hani / at sölum Heljar. <sup>44</sup>Geyr nú Garmr mjök / fyr Gnipahelli, / festr mun slitna, / en freki renna; / fjölð veit ek fræða, / fram sé ek lengra / um ragna rök / römm sigtíva. <sup>45</sup>Bræðr munu berjask / ok at bönum verðask, / munu systrungar / sifjum spilla; / hart er í heimi, / hórdómr mikill, / skeggöld, skalmöld, / skildir ro klofnir, / vindöld, vargöld, / áðr veröld steypisk; / mun engi maðr / öðrum þyrma. <sup>46</sup>Leika Míms synir, / en mjötuðr kyndisk / at inu galla / Gjallarhorni; / hátt blæss Heimdallr, / horn er á lofti, / mælir Óðinn / við Míms höfuð.
translation.text: <sup>31</sup>I saw of Baldr, the blood-stained god, Odin's son, the hidden fate. There stood grown up, high on the plain, slender and passing fair, the mistletoe. <sup>32-33</sup>From that shrub was made, as to me it seemed, a deadly, noxious dart. Hödr shot it forth; but Frigg bewailed, in Fensalir, Valhall's calamity. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>34</sup>Then the Vala knew the fatal bonds were twisting, most rigid, bonds from entrails made. <sup>35</sup>Bound she saw lying, under Hveralund, a monstrous form, to Loki like. There sits Sigyn, for her consort's sake, not right glad. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>36</sup>From the east a river falls, through venom dales, with mire and clods, Slîd is its name. <sup>37</sup>On the north there stood, on Nida-fells, a hall of gold, for Sindri's race; and another stood in Okôlnir, the Jötuns beer-hall which Brîmir hight. <sup>38</sup>She saw a hall standing, far from the sun, in Nâströnd; its doors are northward turned, venom-drops fall in through its apertures: entwined is that hall with serpents' backs. <sup>39</sup>She there saw wading the sluggish streams bloodthirsty men and perjurers, and him who the ear beguiles of another's wife. There Nidhögg sucks the corpses of the dead; the wolf tears men. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>40</sup>East sat the crone, in Iârnvidir, and there reared up Fenrir's progeny: of all shall be one especially the moon's devourer, in a troll's semblance. <sup>41</sup>He is sated with the last breath of dying men; the god's seat he with red gore defiles: swart is the sunshine then for summers after; all weather turns to storm. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>42</sup>There on a height sat, striking a harp, the giantess's watch, the joyous Egdir; by him crowed, in the bird-wood, the bright red cock, which Fialar hight. <sup>43</sup>Crowed o'er the Æsir Gullinkambi, which wakens heroes with the sire of hosts; but another crows beneath the earth, a soot-red cock, in the halls of Hel. <sup>44</sup>Further forward I see, much can I say of Ragnarök and the gods' conflict. <sup>45</sup>Brothers shall fight, and slay each other; cousins shall kinship violate. The earth resounds, the giantesses flee; no man will another spare. Hard is it in the world, great whoredom, an axe age, a sword age, shields shall be cloven, a wind age, a wolf age, ere the world sinks. <sup>46</sup>Mim's sons dance, but the central tree takes fire at the resounding Giallar-horn. Loud blows Heimdall, his horn is raised; Odin speaks with Mim's head.

Fol. 2v (manuscript page 4; handrit.is image 13; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 4, caption 'Vǫluspá v. 45-61'): the top of the page finishes stanza 46 ('hátt blæss Heimdallr ...'). Checked on the image: the first line of fol. 2r has 'Nú eru talðar' (end of Völuspá 30); the first line of fol. 2v has 'hátt blæss Heimdallr' (end of Völuspá 46).

translation.original_text: <sup>47</sup>Skelfr Yggdrasils / askr standandi, / ymr it aldna tré, / en jötunn losnar; / hræðask allir / á helvegum / áðr Surtar þann / sefi of gleypir. <sup>48</sup>Hvat er með ásum? / Hvat er með alfum? / Gnýr allr Jötunheimr, / æsir ro á þingi, / stynja dvergar / fyr steindurum, / veggbergs vísir. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>49</sup>Geyr nú Garmr mjök / fyr Gnipahelli, / festr mun slitna / en freki renna; / fjölð veit ek fræða, / fram sé ek lengra / um ragna rök / römm sigtíva. <sup>50</sup>Hrymr ekr austan, / hefisk lind fyrir, / snýsk Jörmungandr / í jötunmóði; / ormr knýr unnir, / en ari hlakkar, / slítr nái niðfölr, / Naglfar losnar. <sup>51</sup>Kjóll ferr austan, / koma munu Múspells / of lög lýðir, / en Loki stýrir; / fara fíflmegir / með freka allir, / þeim er bróðir / Býleists í för. <sup>52</sup>Surtr ferr sunnan / með sviga lævi, / skínn af sverði / sól valtíva; / grjótbjörg gnata, / en gífr rata, / troða halir helveg, / en himinn klofnar. <sup>53</sup>Þá kemr Hlínar / harmr annarr fram, / er Óðinn ferr / við ulf vega, / en bani Belja / bjartr at Surti; / þá mun Friggjar / falla angan. <sup>54</sup>Geyr nú Garmr mjök / fyr Gnipahelli, / festr mun slitna, / en freki renna; / fjölð veit ek fræða, / fram sé ek lengra / um ragna rök / römm sigtíva. <sup>55</sup>Þá kemr inn mikli / mögr Sigföður, / Víðarr, vega / at valdýri. / Lætr hann megi Hveðrungs / mundum standa / hjör til hjarta, / þá er hefnt föður. <sup>56</sup>Þá kemr inn mæri / mögr Hlóðynjar, / gengr Óðins sonr / við orm vega, / drepr af móði / Miðgarðs véurr, / munu halir allir / heimstöð ryðja; / gengr fet níu / Fjörgynjar burr / neppr frá naðri / níðs ókvíðnum. <sup>57</sup>Sól tér sortna, / sígr fold í mar, / hverfa af himni / heiðar stjörnur; / geisar eimi / ok aldrnari, / leikr hár hiti / við himin sjalfan. <sup>58</sup>Geyr nú Garmr mjök / fyr Gnipahelli, / festr mun slitna / en freki renna; / fjölð veit ek fræða / fram sé ek lengra / um ragna rök / römm sigtíva. <sup>59</sup>Sér hon upp koma / öðru sinni / jörð ór ægi / iðjagræna; / falla forsar, / flýgr örn yfir, / sá er á fjalli / fiska veiðir. <sup>60</sup>Finnask æsir / á Iðavelli / ok um moldþinur / máttkan dæma / ok minnask þar / á megindóma / ok á Fimbultýs / fornar rúnir. <sup>61</sup>Þar munu eftir / undrsamligar / gullnar töflur / í grasi finnask, / þærs í árdaga / áttar höfðu. <sup>62</sup>Munu ósánir / akrar vaxa, / böls mun alls batna, / Baldr mun koma; / búa þeir Höðr ok Baldr / Hrofts sigtoftir, / vé valtíva. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>63</sup>Þá kná Hænir / hlautvið kjósa / ok burir byggja / bræðra tveggja / vindheim víðan. / Vituð ér enn - eða hvat? <sup>64</sup>Sal sér hon standa / sólu fegra, / gulli þakðan / á Gimléi; / þar skulu dyggvar / dróttir byggja / ok um aldrdaga / ynðis njóta.
translation.text: <sup>47</sup>Trembles Yggdrasil's ash yet standing; groans that aged tree, and the jötun is loosed. Loud bays Garm before the Gnupa-cave, his bonds he rends asunder; and the wolf runs. <sup>48</sup>How is it with the Æsir? How with the Alfar? All Jötunheim resounds; the Æsir are in council. The dwarfs groan before their stony doors, the sages of the rocky walls. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>50</sup>Hrym steers from the east, the waters rise, the mundane snake is coiled in jötun-rage. The worm beats the water, and the eagle screams: the pale of beak tears carcases; Naglfar is loosed. <sup>51</sup>That ship fares from the east: come will Muspell's people o'er the sea, and Loki steers. The monster's kin goes all with the wolf; with them the brother is of Byleist on their course. <sup>52</sup>Surt from the south comes with flickering flame; shines from his sword the Val-gods' sun. The stony hills are dashed together, the giantesses totter; men tread the path of Hel, and heaven is cloven. <sup>53</sup>Then arises Hlîn's second grief, when Odin goes with the wolf to fight, and the bright slayer of Beli with Surt. Then will Frigg's beloved fall. <sup>55</sup>Then comes the great victor-sire's son, Vidar, to fight with the deadly beast. He with his hands will make his sword pierce to the heart of the giant's son: then avenges he his father. <sup>56</sup>Then comes the mighty son of Hlôdyn: (Odin's son goes with the monster to fight); Midgârd's Veor in his rage will slay the worm. Nine feet will go Fiörgyn's son, bowed by the serpent, who feared no foe. All men will their homes forsake. <sup>57</sup>The sun darkens, earth in ocean sinks, fall from heaven the bright stars, fire's breath assails the all-nourishing tree, towering fire plays against heaven itself. <sup>59</sup>She sees arise, a second time, earth from ocean, beauteously green, waterfalls descending; the eagle flying over, which in the fell captures fish. <sup>60</sup>The Æsir meet on Ida's plain, and of the mighty earth-encircler speak, and there to memory call their mighty deeds, and the supreme god's ancient lore. <sup>61</sup>There shall again the wondrous golden tables in the grass be found, which in days of old had possessed the ruler of the gods, and Fiölnir's race. <sup>62</sup>Unsown shall the fields bring forth, all evil be amended; Baldr shall come; Hödr and Baldr, the heavenly gods, Hropt's glorious dwellings shall inhabit. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>63</sup>Then can Hoenir choose his lot, and the two brothers' sons inhabit the spacious Vindheim. Understand ye yet, or what? <sup>64</sup>She a hall standing than the sun brighter, with gold bedecked, in Gimill: there shall be righteous people dwell, and for evermore happiness enjoy.

Fol. 3r (manuscript page 5; handrit.is image 14; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 5, caption 'Vǫluspá v. 61 - Hávamál v. 15'): the top of the page finishes stanza 64 ('dróttir byggja ...'). Checked on the image: the first line of fol. 2v has 'hátt blæss Heimdallr' (end of Völuspá 46); the first line of fol. 3r has 'dróttir byggja' (end of Völuspá 64). Stanza 54 (the Garmr refrain) is not written at this point in Codex Regius: on fol. 2v stanza 53 is followed directly by stanza 55. Guðni Jónsson repeats the refrain here after Hauksbók. On fol. 2v the manuscript order is 47, refrain (abbreviated 'Geyr nú g.'), 50, 51, 48, 52, 53, 55, 56, 57, refrain ('Geyr n.'), 59-64; the edition moves stanza 48 and writes the refrain out in full as stanzas 49 and 58.

translation.original_text: <sup>65</sup>Þá kemr inn ríki / at regindómi / öflugr ofan, / sá er öllu ræðr. <sup>66</sup>Þar kemr inn dimmi / dreki fljúgandi, / naðr fránn, neðan / frá Niðafjöllum; / berr sér í fjöðrum, / - flýgr völl yfir, - / Niðhöggr nái. / Nú mun hon sökkvask.
translation.text: <sup>65</sup>Then comes the mighty one to the great judgment, the powerful from above, who rules o'er all. He shall dooms pronounce, and strifes allay, holy peace establish, which shall ever be. <sup>66</sup>There comes the dark dragon flying from beneath the glistening serpent, from Nida-fels. On his wings bears Nidhögg, flying o'er the plain, a corpse. Now she will descend.
translation.scan_note: Fol. 3r (manuscript page 5; handrit.is image 14; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 5, caption 'Vǫluspá v. 61 - Hávamál v. 15'): stanza 66 begins here. Checked on the image: the first line of fol. 3r has 'dróttir byggja' (end of Völuspá 64). Stanza 65 (Þá kemr inn ríki) is not in Codex Regius: on fol. 3r stanza 64 is followed directly by stanza 66. Guðni Jónsson's text takes it from Hauksbók (AM 544 4to); fol. 3r is linked because that is where the stanza would stand.

translator_notes: Thorpe printed the middle of the poem in a different order from the manuscript, and the old version of this entry set his stanzas beside the wrong Old Norse stanzas from stanza 21 on. Each Thorpe stanza now stands beside the Old Norse stanza it translates. His numbers differ as follows (Old Norse = Thorpe): 21=25, 22=26, 23=27, 24=28, 25=29, 26=30, 27=31, 28=21+22, 29=23, 30=24, 31=36, 32-33=37, 34=39, 35=38, 36=40, 37=41, 38=42, 39=43, 40=32, 41=33, 42=34, 43=35, 45=45+46, 46=47, 47=48 (which also renders the Garmr refrain), 48=52, 50=49, 51=50, 52=51, 55=54, 56=55, 57=56, 59=57, 60=58, 61=59, 62=60, 63=61, 64=62, 65=64, 66=65. Thorpe has no separate English for the repeated refrain (49, 54, 58), and his translation lacks parts of stanzas 32-33 (Baldrs bróðir ... Baldrs andskota).

Stanza 65 (Þá kemr inn ríki) is not in Codex Regius: on fol. 3r stanza 64 is followed directly by stanza 66. Guðni Jónsson's text takes it from Hauksbók (AM 544 4to); fol. 3r is linked because that is where the stanza would stand.
Stanza 54 (the Garmr refrain) is not written at this point in Codex Regius: on fol. 2v stanza 53 is followed directly by stanza 55. Guðni Jónsson repeats the refrain here after Hauksbók.
